🤖 Happy Black Friday! My Instinct (an agentic personal assistant) is a pusher. This morning it texted: "It's Black Friday. Anything you've been meaning to buy that you'd like me to find a deal on?" No! Sleep in!

  • Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 693 words, a 2½-min. read. Thanks to Bill Kole for copy editing.
 
 
1 big thing: Next year's travel hot spots
 
Data: Kayak. Chart: Alex Fitzpatrick/Axios

Cities in Guatemala, Morocco and El Salvador are among the 10 highest-trending international destinations for 2027 travel, Alex Fitzpatrick writes from new Kayak data.

  • That's thanks to new hotels and flight routes, travelers' desire to make their money go further, and, in Morocco's case, early interest ahead of the 2030 World Cup.

💸 Kayak's Kayla DeLoache tells Axios of the top-10 list: "The average flight price might be high for some of these destinations ... but when you get there, your dollar stretches further. You can get some really great hotel nightly rates."

How it works: Kayak's data is based on U.S. searches made between April 1 and Sept. 25 of this year for travel any time next year, compared to the same period a year prior.

  • These "trending" destinations had the biggest bumps in search interest.

Zoom out: Tokyo, Cancún and London are Kayak's most-searched foreign cities overall for travel in 2027.

😎 Between the lines: Expedia says 2027 will be the year of "Un-Adulting," with travelers looking to "escape from adult responsibilities and go on carefree vacations full of childlike joy."

  • It's also seeing a rise in one-night stays — what it's calling "trip snacking."

What's next: Kayak and similar platforms have been rolling out new AI features designed to help travelers plan their trips using both old-school search and new natural-language options.

  • Where to go in 2027.
 
 
2. 🤖 Doctors vs. AI
 
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images

Doctors who disagree with AI could be in greater danger of losing a malpractice suit, Axios' Adriel Bettelheim reports from a new study.

  • In simulated court cases, researchers found that mock juries were more likely to side with plaintiffs in malpractice suits when AI disagreed with radiologists.

🧠 One scenario involved a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage.

  • When AI flagged the condition but the radiologist didn't think there was a problem, the jurors sided with the plaintiff nearly 75% of the time, the researchers wrote in NEJM AI.

Yes, but: A smaller share of jurors ruled against the physician when they were told about the AI system's error rate.

3. ⚡️ Catch me up
 
Shoppers pour into Macy's Herald Square in New York this morning. Photo: Adam Gray/AP
  1. 🛒 We're still doing that Black Friday thing: Despite weeks of online deals, people lined up before sunrise at the flagship Macy's Herald Square in Manhattan, with some filming on their phones as they burst in. Sensormatic, which tracks retail foot traffic, says Black Friday continues to draw more store visits than any other day. Keep reading.
  2. 📚 Former President Biden's "Promise Me, America" sold around 21,000 copies during its debut week, according to Circana, which tracks about 85% of hardcover sales. The book hit No. 1 on The New York Times hardcover nonfiction bestseller list but didn't approach the sales of memoirs by Barack Obama and Bill Clinton. More from AP.
  3. 💻 Hackers breached the Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, which could jeopardize sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data, Reuters reports. The intrusion at Cloud One was ‌discovered within the past month or so during upgrade work. The Air Force said it "does not comment on the ​security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems." Keep reading.
 
 
4. 🚁 1 for the road: Drones find lost pets
 
Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios

Some pet owners are turning to drones to find their lost animals, Axios Dallas' Ned Oliver reports.

📈 Demand for drone searches took off this year, says Drew Smith of Overhead Perspectives in Weatherford, Texas.

  • His drones use thermal cameras to pick up an animal's heat signature from above, covering hundreds of acres far faster than a search on foot.

🐶 Smith recalls one woman whose two dogs had been gone for about 25 hours in a heavily wooded area. "Within five minutes, I'd located the dogs," he says.

  • He's also searched for cats and, once, a calf that got something stuck on its head and wandered into dense brush.
